title: More ways to use scalar UDFs in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
text: Scalar user-defined functions (UDFs) let data teams define a business rule once and reuse it across workloads in both Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint in Microsoft Fabric. This helps teams maintain consistent logic without duplicating it across queries. Some business rules require more than a single expression. They use procedural logic such as conditional branches, multiple RETURN statements, or WHILE loops. Expression Block inlining compiles and executes this logic in a distributed manner, helping reusable functions scale across analytical workloads. Building on that foundation, this update brings several improvements: More natural loop control and broader query-shape support. Automatic adoption of newly supported capabilities by existing functions, without recreating or altering them. Inlineability validation for new or changed functions, with diagnostics that explain any gaps and an explicit WITH INLINE = AUTO override when a non-inlineable function is acceptable. Express loop intent with BREAK and CONTINUE Loops often need to skip the rest of the current iteration or stop processing entirely. Without CONTINUE and BREAK, developers typically rely on extra flags, nested IF blocks, or repeated conditions. Those workarounds make the control flow harder to read and more difficult to update safely. Consider a function that standardizes tracking codes received from carrier and warehouse systems. Formatting characters such as spaces, hyphens, and slashes should be ignored. A pipe character marks the beginning of an operational note, so the function should stop there. CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.fn_NormalizeTrackingCode (@Input VARCHAR(MAX) ) RETURNS VARCHAR(MAX) AS BEGIN IF @Input IS NULL RETURN NULL; DECLARE @Result VARCHAR(MAX) = ''; DECLARE @Character VARCHAR(1); DECLARE @Position INT = 1; WHILE @Position BEGIN SET @Character = SUBSTRING(@Input, @Position, 1); SET @Position = @Position + 1; IF @Character = '|' BREAK ; IF @Character = ' ' OR @Character = '-' OR @Character = '/' CONTINUE ; SET @Result = @Result + UPPER(@Character); END; RETURN @Result; END; In this example, CONTINUE skips formatting characters, while BREAK stops processing when the operational note begins. The function therefore follows the business rule without a separate stop flag or another level of nesting. For an input such as "northwind-1000 / 1234 | imported from partner API", the function returns "NORTHWIND10001234". Use large-value data types in more query shapes The example uses VARCHAR(MAX) for both the parameter and the return type. Previously, MAX data types relied on Scalar UDF inlining and were subject to its calling-query restrictions. Expression Block inlining now supports VARCHAR(MAX), NVARCHAR(MAX), and VARBINARY(MAX) parameters, local variables, and return values. The function can keep its MAX types and be called from various query shapes. The following CTE is one example: it standardizes each event, then summarizes the number of source formats and standardized codes for each carrier. WITH StandardizedEvents AS ( SELECT ShipmentId, CarrierCode, RawTrackingCode, dbo.fn_NormalizeTrackingCode(RawTrackingCode) AS StandardizedCode FROM dbo.TrackingEvents WHERE RawTrackingCode IS NOT NULL ) SELECT CarrierCode, COUNT_BIG(*) AS EventCount, COUNT(DISTINCT RawTrackingCode) AS RawCodeCount, COUNT(DISTINCT StandardizedCode) AS StandardizedCodeCount FROM StandardizedEvents GROUP BY CarrierCode ORDER BY CarrierCode; You no longer need to choose between retaining MAX parameters and return types and using the query structure that best expresses your intent. Call scalar UDFs in IF EXISTS queries Procedural batches frequently need to ask whether any row meets a reusable business rule before taking the next action. The query inside IF EXISTS can now call a scalar UDF that uses Expression Block inlining. The following statement checks whether the tracking event table contains a specific standardized code. The function owns the normalization rule, while the batch owns the decision about what to do when a matching row exists. IF EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM dbo.TrackingEvents WHERE dbo.fn_NormalizeTrackingCode(RawTrackingCode) = 'NORTHWIND10001234' ) BEGIN SELECT 'Matching shipment found' AS ValidationResult; END ELSE BEGIN SELECT 'No matching shipment found' AS ValidationResult; END; This pattern keeps the existence check set-based and keeps the reusable scalar logic in one function. It is useful for validation gates, conditional batch steps, data-quality checks, and orchestration procedures that need to branch on the presence of qualifying rows. Existing functions gain new capabilities automatically As inlining support expands, your existing UDFs can become inlineable, run more efficiently, or become available in additional query shapes without being recreated or altered. The function text remains the same, while its current inlineability is reflected in the sys.sql_modules catalog view. SELECT SCHEMA_NAME(o.schema_id) AS FunctionSchema, o.name AS FunctionName, m.is_inlineable AS IsInlineable, m.inline_eligibility_mask AS InlineEligibilityMask FROM sys.objects AS o INNER JOIN sys.sql_modules AS m ON o.object_id = m.object_id WHERE o.type = 'FN'; The is_inlineable value indicates whether the function can be inlined, and inline_eligibility_mask identifies the applicable inlining technique. Check these values to confirm current service behavior because a function’s eligibility can change as inlining support expands. Default inlineability checks with an explicit override CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION now checks inlineability by default. When a definition does not meet the inlining requirements, the statement is rejected, and the error identifies what prevents inlining. This catches compatibility gaps when the function is defined, before it can be referenced by a query. When a non-inlineable function is acceptable given its business context, WITH INLINE = AUTO explicitly overrides the default creation requirement. For example, the following function reads a table and uses multiple RETURN statements. It can still be useful as a standalone existence check even though it is not inlineable. CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.fn_HasTrackingEvents (@CarrierCode VARCHAR(20)) RETURNS BIT WITH INLINE = AUTO AS BEGIN IF EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM dbo.TrackingEvents WHERE CarrierCode = @CarrierCode ) RETURN 1; RETURN 0; END; WITH INLINE = AUTO does not make a function inlineable or change the execution behavior of a function that is already inlineable. It explicitly allows creation of an intentionally non-inlineable standalone function. What's next Existing functions gain these capabilities automatically. First, check their status in the system catalog, then test the new query shapes with your procedural scalar UDFs. For the current syntax, metadata, and inlining requirements, refer to CREATE FUNCTION for Fabric Data Warehouse . For a guided introduction, refer to Create scalar user-defined functions in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse . To share a specific scenario or feedback, email Fabric DW functions feedback .

title: Build clearer, more expressive Real-Time Dashboards with new design and KPI capabilities (Generally Available)
text: The new, generally available authoring capabilities in Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Dashboards help authors create dashboards that are easier to scan and act on. Design Tiles add structure and context, multi-KPI groups related measures from one query, and KPI styling makes status, scale, and targets easier to interpret. Together, these capabilities give viewers a clear path from context to metrics to investigation while reducing repetitive authoring work. Figure: Camp Nou Stadium Operations Center dashboard using Design Tiles, Multi-KPI, and styled KPIs. Give your dashboard a clear structure with Design Tiles A dashboard can contain accurate visuals and still make viewers work too hard to find what matters. As service health, deployment status, business metrics, and diagnostic details accumulate, Design Tiles provide the structure, and context viewers need to identify priorities and move quickly to the right information. Design Tiles provide three focused building blocks directly on the Real-Time Dashboard canvas: Title adds a dashboard heading or a short section label. Figure: Title tile in Editing mode, with the formatting toolbar. Text Box adds descriptions, operational guidance, annotations, and links. Figure: Text Box tile with contact details and links. Divider creates a labeled horizontal break between dashboard sections. Figure: Divider tile labeled “Gates Drill Down.” Authors can add a Title, Text Box, or Divider from the top toolbar in Editing mode. Titles and Text Boxes are ready for direct editing on the canvas, so authors can add context and guidance without leaving the dashboard or opening a separate configuration experience. Inline editing keeps formatting work on the canvas. Title formatting applies to the entire title, while Text Box formatting can be applied to selected text or to the text entered next. Authors can also add links and apply a background to the Text Box. Design Tiles use theme-aware, accessible colors and support keyboard navigation. Text pasted into a Text Box is handled in a way that helps prevent unsupported formatting or content from disrupting the dashboard. Show related metrics together with multi-KPI Operational questions often produce several related values, such as error rate by service, volume by region, or overall fleet health. Building a separate query and tile for each value creates repetitive authoring work, consumes dashboard space, and makes related metrics harder to compare. Multi-KPI addresses those problems by presenting the results together in one visual. Multi-KPI lets one query produce many KPI items in a single visual. It handles two common query results: When the query returns labeled rows, each row becomes a KPI, and its label value becomes the item label. When the query returns to a single row with several numeric columns, each numeric column becomes a KPI, and its column name becomes the item label. This behavior lets you use the natural result of a KQL aggregation without rewriting it for presentation. A summary by service can become one KPI per service, while named aggregate columns can become a compact operational summary. The visual uses labels from the query results and applies a shared configuration across all KPI items. Choose Number, Bar, Gauge, or Donut, then configure value format, scale, thresholds, colors, and directionality once for the entire set. This shared treatment makes related metrics easier to scan and compare. You can control the maximum number of items and how they are arranged. The layout adapts as you resize the tiles. At smaller sizes, each KPI displays its value and status of color, and viewers can point to a shortened label to see the full text in a tooltip. When more space is available, the visual displays full labels and supporting details. Figure: Multi-KPI gauges for seven gates, generated from one query. Match each KPI to the metric and the available space Some metrics need a quick status signal. Others are best shown as an exact value or as progress toward a target. The same four KPI styles are available for individual KPI tiles and multi-KPI visuals, so you can choose the treatment that best fits the metric and the available space: Number emphasizes the formatted value and works well in dense summary areas. Bar shows progress along a horizontal range and fits short, horizontal tiles. Gauge uses an arc to show the current value within a range. Donut uses a full ring and works well in square layouts. Gauge styling can be adapted to different layouts and visual priorities. Choose a 180°, 220°, or 270° arc, adjust its weight with Band thickness, select flat or rounded ends with Cap style, and use Gradient fill to control the color transition. Figure: Gauge styling controls for Arc angle, Band thickness, Cap style, and Gradient fill. Thresholds define healthy, warning, and critical ranges. Directionality determines whether higher or lower values indicate declining performance. For example, a higher error rate can be worse, while lower throughput can be worse. This ensures that the status of treatment reflects how each metric should be interpreted. A reference line can show a target, baseline, or expected value. Value formatting controls let you choose decimal precision, thousands of separators, or compact notation such as 1.2K. Used together, these settings help viewers answer both “What is the value?” and “How should I interpret it?” at a glance. Build one coherent operational story The three capabilities are most useful when you treat them as parts of one authoring workflow. Start with structure. Add a Title that names the operational area and a short Text Box that explains the time range, threshold policy, or expected response. Use a Divider when the dashboard moves from a high-level summary to investigation details. Next, use multi-KPI for metrics that share a query context and presentation model. A single query can show the top services by failures or a set of aggregate health measures. Set a maximum item count that keeps labels readable and choose the KPI style that communicates with the group most clearly. Finally, reserve individual KPI tiles for measures that deserve stronger emphasis or a distinct visual treatment. The styles work the same way here: use Number for a precise headline, Bar for a horizontal progress view, or Gauge and Donut for range-based status. Apply thresholds, directionality, a reference line, and value formatting consistently with the explanation you placed on the dashboard. Viewers get a reading path; related metrics stay together, and important values use treatments that match their meaning. Authors spend less time repeating queries and formatting work. Get started You can add these capabilities to an existing dashboard in a few steps, then evaluate the result at the size and layout your audience normally uses: Open an existing Real-Time Dashboard in Editing mode so you can add structure, group related metrics, and refine KPI presentation. Add a Title, Text Box, or Divider from the top toolbar, then use it to establish the dashboard hierarchy, explain important context, or separate sections. Add a multi-KPI visual for a query that returns labeled rows or a single row with several numeric columns, then use the visual to compare those related results in one place. Figure: Add visual menu in Editing mode, with Multi KPI available next to KPI, Time Series, and other visual types. Choose a shared KPI style and configuration, set the maximum number of items, and resize the tile to confirm that labels and values remain readable. Use an individual KPI tile for a metric that needs stronger emphasis, then select Number, Bar, Gauge, or Donut and configure the formatting, thresholds, directionality, and reference value that help viewers interpret it. Save the dashboard and review it at the size your audience normally uses. Confirm that viewers can identify priorities, interpret status of colors and thresholds, and find supporting guidance wit

title: On-premises data gateway October 2026 release
text: The October 2026 release of the on-premises data gateway (version 3000.338) continues our commitment to secure, reliable and accessible connectivity between on-premises data sources and Microsoft Fabric services. This release focuses on accessibility, configuration reliability, and troubleshooting. It makes the installer and configurator more inclusive, keeps your Power Query settings intact during connection tests, and makes service-start failures easier to diagnose. It also brings compatibility updates for the October 2026 release of Power BI Desktop, so queries run the same way in Power BI Desktop and in cloud refreshes. General improvements and fixes The October 2026 Gateway release (3000.338) includes Power Query Engine 2.159.229 and introduces the following improvements: Accessibility improvements in the installer and configurator Building on the accessibility work in the September release, this update improves the experience for users who rely on assistive technologies: Keyboard navigation: Moving through the gateway installer and configurator with the keyboard is smoother and more predictable. Screen-reader announcements: Screen readers now give clearer, more accurate announcements of controls, status changes and actions. High-contrast support: Readability and visual consistency are better when Windows high-contrast themes are on. Power Query configuration settings preserved during connection tests Running a connection test no longer affects your Power Query configuration settings. They stay as you set them, so you can validate connectivity without reapplying your configuration afterward. Better diagnostics for gateway service-start failures When the gateway service fails to start, it now provides more detailed diagnostics. Administrators can find the root cause faster and restore connectivity with less downtime. Feature updates and new capabilities in OPDG: Admin APIs for connections and gateways (Preview) Managing connections at scale is a priority for many organizations. Until now, administrators could only see the connections they had been given permission for, which made tenant-wide governance difficult. The new Admin Connections REST APIs give Fabric administrators full visibility and control over every connection in the tenant, including on-premises data gateway, virtual network gateway and cloud connections. These APIs can be called by Fabric administrators or by service principals, so you can automate governance and audit workflows. Admin actions such as viewing or deleting a connection and changing role assignments are recorded in the audit logs for traceability. Learn more in the related documentation. Power BI Desktop compatibility This update brings the on-premises data gateway up to date with the October 2026 release of Power BI Desktop. Download on-premises data gateway (standard mode) Download on-premises data gateway (personal mode) With this version of the gateway, reports you publish to the Power BI Service and refresh through the gateway use the same query execution logic and runtime as the October version of Power BI Desktop. Best practices for upgrading your gateway Some customers have told us they upgraded production gateways straight to a new release and then ran into unexpected issues, such as failed refreshes or connection errors. Most of these can be avoided by upgrading in stages. We strongly recommend validating every new gateway release in a lower environment before you upgrade production. Explore the following best practices: Start with a development or test environment : Install version 3000.338 on a non-production gateway that matches your production setup as closely as possible: the same data sources, connectors, authentication methods and network setup. This lets you catch compatibility issues before they reach business-critical workloads. Validate your key scenarios in the test environment : Confirm that the scenarios your organization depends on still work as expected: Scheduled and on-demand refreshes for your critical semantic models and dataflows DirectQuery and live connection reports Connection tests for each data source type you use Any custom connectors, if you use them Gateway service start-up and sign-in Monitor before you promote : Give the test gateway a representative period, such as a few refresh cycles, before you move on. Review refresh history, gateway logs and performance to spot any regressions early. Back up before upgrading production : Before you upgrade a production gateway, make sure the gateway recovery key is stored securely and you have a record of your gateway configuration. You'll need these if you have to restore or migrate the gateway. Upgrade production clusters one member at a time : If you run gateway clusters, upgrade one member at a time while the other members keep serving requests. Confirm each upgraded member is healthy before moving to the next. Keep all members of a cluster on the same version when you're done, because mixed versions can lead to inconsistent behavior. Schedule production upgrades during a maintenance window : Plan production upgrades for periods of low refresh activity and let stakeholders know ahead of time. That way, any unexpected issue has minimal business impact. Stay on a supported version : Microsoft supports only the last six releases of the on-premises data gateway. Upgrading regularly keeps you on a supported version with the latest security, reliability and accessibility improvements. Next steps Upgrade to version 3000.338 to get the latest accessibility, configuration reliability and diagnostics improvements. Please share feedback and feature requests through the Power BI Ideas forum to help shape future gateway investments. Thank you!

title: Data Visualization in the Agentic Era
text: Data visualizations help people identify patterns, trends, and outliers in their data. However, creating a useful visual requires several decisions: which chart and data to use, how to map the data to visual properties such as color and position, and how the finished visual should look. AI-assisted development can reduce that complexity by letting developers describe the intended result in natural language while reusable visualization components handle common design and interaction requirements. Deciding what visualization to create is one problem, while deciding how to create it is another. Power BI offers a convenient way to create reports and visualizations, but authors work within the chart types and formatting options that the product provides. AI coding agents another approach: developers can describe a visualization in natural language and optionally provide example images. Developers no longer have to start with a custom visual implementation or a visualization or graphics specification. Hello! I’m Alper, a data visualization engineer who joined the Power BI Core Visuals team after completing my PhD at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 2017. My academic research concentrated on the way we summarize data for visualization and how that affects the analysis tasks that viewers can perform with those visuals. At Microsoft, I have contributed to the development of visualization- and report-related features, as well as continued research in accessible representations of data visualizations. You can learn more about this work on my website . My goal is to ensure that people can realize the potential of visualizations to improve their understanding of data, democratizing access to data without requiring specialized development expertise. Agentic data app development with a generic visualization library advances this goal, and I’m happy to share the progress in this blog post. Coding agents can now generate data visualization specifications from natural-language prompts. For example, a prompt such as “show me outliers in my sales data” can produce a scatter plot that reveals the overall trend while making unusual values easier to identify. Figure: An example scatter plot generated from the query “show me outliers in my sales data”, plotting quantity in an order vs sales amount, broken down by country. Points in the top-right quadrant of the chart represent relatively expensive orders of a high quantity of items. AI coding agents can generate visualizations from several types of specifications. For the analytics template we’ve released alongside Rayfin , our Fabric visuals library depends on the established Vega-Lite specification language . We chose Vega-Lite as our foundational specification because it has a strong research history (beginning with the initial IEEE VIS 2017 paper ), a large collection of public examples , and a proven, stable ecosystem . A Vega-Lite specification is pretty straightforward even for a human to read! A bar chart may look something like the following: { "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v6.json", "title": "WW Gross by Studio", "data": { "name": "movieStudioDataset" }, "mark": "bar", "encoding": { "y": { "field": "Studio/Distributor", "sort": "-x" }, "x": { "field": "WW Gross", "aggregate": "sum" } } } When passed through the Vega-Lite library, the following visualization is rendered: Figure: A bar chart generated from the Vega-Lite specification above. Bars show worldwide box office gross by a selection of production companies. You may notice from the JSON specification above that we bind columns of our dataset to visual channels , such as the x - and y -axis. This means that every row of data is evaluated against this binding to create visual marks representing that item. We can also bind data to other visual encodings, like color , angle , line , area , and repetition elements like row and column to make heatmap and small multiple visualizations. You can also see that the above spec uses an aggregate definition, which sums the measure against each unique category, rolling up and summing multiple data rows if they have the same category. This approach is highly flexible because it represents repeated layouts of data-driven shapes in an abstract, graphics-independent specification. Instead of selecting only from predefined chart types such as pie or line charts, developers can compose a wider range of visual forms. Our visualization libraries for AI-first workflows We created reusable React components to help developers build analytics apps with Fabric data. The Fabric visuals package supports the creation of charts and the Fabric data grid supports tabular experiences. Both packages are available on npm and are designed to give developers and AI agents a consistent starting point instead of requiring a rebuild of core behavior for every app. We consider these packages to be in preview as we work to ensure best-in-class support for accessibility, functionality, and world readiness. As part of the design and development process for this visualization library, our team wanted to ensure that the specifications generated by AI agents make sense for the visual that users want. It is relatively straightforward to ask an agent to generate a visualization. However, by making the design, construction, and layout of visualizations opinionated, we can push toward better visualization design with the features users expect from viewing and interacting with data visualizations. These opinions allow us to support features that users expect from visualizations. Features such as column format strings, app theming instructions, and a consistent design between multiple visuals and tables all become natively supported. This support circumvents the need for the AI agents (or humans!) to reinvent core functionality in every app generation. Visuals generated entirely by AI agents can be isolated, noninteractive, and inconsistently styled. They may also fail to meet functional and regulatory requirements, including accessibility requirements. Power BI visuals already address many of these needs, but their implementation is too closely tied to the report infrastructure to be extracted directly as reusable components. Our features and design motivation When designing our components around Vega-Lite, we wanted to support behavior and design guardrails to improve specifications generated by both developers and AI agents. We found that adapting the Power BI visual style to a Vega configuration was not enough to produce a consistently clean experience. We therefore built these behaviors into the components so developers and AI agents do not have to implement them separately, reducing development time and cost. From how we know people use visualizations in Power BI reports, we knew that we wanted rich support for data displayed in tables. Therefore, a primary focus is to ensure that many different types of data are supported in our data grid component. Specifically, we support visualizing data with data bars, images that can expand to fill the screen on click, and an extendable adapter to visualize rich text or other arbitrary data-driven item within grid cells. Our data grid implementation also supports filtering, reordering, sorting, and resizing columns out of the box. We wanted a consistent design language, so we adapted to Segoe UI text, 3-pixel lines, and Power BI data colors. We enforce a minimum distance between bars between categories, add some rounded bar ends, and customize the Vega-Lite’s axes to align more closely with the default Power BI style. title: Announcing workspace monitoring integration for Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
text: With Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse integration with workspace monitoring (Preview), you can analyze completed warehouse query activity across an entire workspace from the monitoring Eventhouse and KQL database, helping you find failed or slow queries and quickly identify the warehouse that needs attention. See warehouse activity across your workspace Monitoring multiple warehouses is difficult when query activity is spread across separate tools and experiences. Workspace monitoring brings completed warehouse execution events into the WarehouseExecutions table, where administrators and operators can review activity across the workspace from a single monitoring database. The integration supports warehouses, SQL analytics endpoints, and warehouse snapshots. It captures completed, user-initiated queries that use distributed execution and records details such as duration, status, result codes, and CPU time. With this information in one place, you can spot failures or performance issues and focus your investigation on the affected warehouse and query. Use this telemetry to: Compare performance: Track query duration trends and percentiles across warehouses and other supported items to identify were performance needs attention. Investigate failures: Analyze failed queries, failure rates, and result codes to identify affected items and isolate the relevant time windows. Understand workload patterns: Compare query volume and CPU time by item and user and create reusable KQL queries or Real-Time Dashboard views for ongoing visibility. Figure: Analyze warehouse query execution telemetry with workspace monitoring. Query warehouse activity across the workspace When workspace monitoring is enabled, Microsoft Fabric creates a read-only monitoring Eventhouse and KQL database for the workspace. Data Warehouse sends supported query execution events for warehouses, SQL analytics endpoints, and warehouse snapshots to the WarehouseExecutions table, giving you one place to analyze completed activity across these items. Each WarehouseExecutions event represents a completed, user-initiated query that uses distributed execution. The event includes identifiers, timing and duration details, CPU time, completion status, result information, and identity data that you can use to filter and investigate activity. Because the data is stored in a KQL database, you can explore it with ad hoc queries, save reusable query sets, or build a Real-Time Dashboard. The following query summarizes activity for each item during the last 24 hours: WarehouseExecutions | where Timestamp > ago(24h) | summarize QueryCount = count(), AverageDurationMs = round(avg(DurationMs), 2), TotalCpuTimeMs = sum(CpuTimeMs) by ItemId, ItemKind | order by TotalCpuTimeMs desc The results provide a workspace-wide view of query volume and CPU usage, helping you identify which items warrant a closer performance, reliability, or workload investigation. Compare query performance across warehouses Warehouses can vary in data volume, number of users, and workload patterns. An average alone can hide whether most queries are slow, or a small number of long-running queries are skewing the overall result. Use duration percentiles to compare the distribution of query performance: WarehouseExecutions | where Timestamp > ago(24h) | summarize QueryCount = count(), AverageDurationMs = round(avg(DurationMs), 2), P50DurationMs = percentile(DurationMs, 50), P95DurationMs = percentile(DurationMs, 95) by ItemId, ItemKind | order by P95DurationMs desc A warehouse with a moderate average duration but a much higher 95th-percentile duration may have a small group of long-running queries. If both the median and 95th-percentile durations are high, the issue may affect the broader workload. After identifying the affected item and UTC time range, use Data Warehouse Monitor or Query Insights for a deeper query-level investigation. Find warehouses with recurring failures Workspace-level failure analysis helps distinguish an isolated query error from a recurring pattern. Use the Status and ResultCode columns to group failures by warehouse and error code. let QueryTotals = WarehouseExecutions | where Timestamp > ago(24h) | summarize TotalQueries = count() by ItemId, ItemKind; let Failures = WarehouseExecutions | where Timestamp > ago(24h) | where Status == "Failed" | summarize FailedQueries = count() by ItemId, ItemKind, ResultCode; Failures | join kind=leftouter QueryTotals on ItemId, ItemKind | extend FailureRatePercent = round(100.0 * FailedQueries / TotalQueries, 2) | project ItemId, ItemKind, ResultCode, FailedQueries, TotalQueries, FailureRatePercent | order by FailedQueries desc This view shows whether one warehouse accounts for most failures or the same result code appear across several items. Use the affected item, result code, and UTC time window to focus the next stage of the investigation. Move from workspace signals to query details Workspace monitoring and Query Insights share the same query execution identifier. The OperationId value in WarehouseExecutions matches distributed_statement_id in queryinsights.exec_requests_history, giving you a direct way to locate the corresponding Query Insights record for deeper analysis. Use the following workflow: Find the affected item and query in WarehouseExecutions. Record the item identifier and OperationId. Open the corresponding warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint. Query queryinsights.exec_requests_history where distributed_statement_id equals the OperationId. Review the query text, query hash, login, status, statement type, duration, CPU time, scan metrics, and SQL pool details. Use the OperationId value in a Query Insights query: Replace the example value with the OperationId from the corresponding WarehouseExecutions event before running the query. SELECT distributed_statement_id, start_time, end_time, login_name, status, total_elapsed_time_ms, allocated_cpu_time_ms, command FROM queryinsights.exec_requests_history WHERE distributed_statement_id = ''; Replace the example value with the OperationId from the corresponding WarehouseExecutions event before running the query. Run this query in the warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint associated with the workspace monitoring event. The shared OperationId value provides an exact lookup when several queries run during the same interval, without relying on approximate duration or timestamp matches. Create reusable monitoring views Save KQL queries for common investigation paths or use the monitoring database as the source for a Real-Time Dashboard. Reusable views help teams track recurring issues and move from workspace-wide trends to the affected item more quickly. Useful dashboard elements include: Query count, failure count, and failure rate. Total and average CPU time by item. Median and 95th-percentile duration by item. Query volume and failures over time. Recent failures grouped by result code. Start with a dashboard time range that matches your operational review cycle. Add item and status filters so viewers can move from workspace-wide trends to one affected item without rewriting the underlying KQL. Each workspace has its own monitoring Eventhouse and KQL database, so the monitoring data remains scoped to that workspace. Use WarehouseExecutions to analyze completed, user-initiated distributed queries across the workspace. For live query investigation and deeper analysis within a specific warehouse, use Data Warehouse Monitor. Next steps Get started by enabling workspace monitoring for your Fabric workspace, then explore the WarehouseExecutions table in the monitoring KQL database. To learn more, see Monitor warehouse activity with workspace monitoring and Use Query Insights in Fabric Data Warehouse .

title: Explore and process multiple event types with Schema-aware Fabric Eventstreams (Preview)
text: Real-time streams rarely contain just one kind of event. A building operations stream, for example, might carry thermostat readings, occupancy updates, air-quality measurements, and badge-reader activity through the same source. These events may share a payload format, but they don't describe the same thing. A temperature field matters to a thermostat event. An employee identifier belongs to an access event. An occupancy count describes something else entirely. Traditionally, processing a mixed stream like this often meant treating it as one wide, sparse schema or reconstructing the meaning of each event downstream. Developers identify the event type, guard against fields that don't apply, and often repeat that logic wherever the stream branches. With Schema-aware Fabric Eventstreams (Preview) , Eventstreams can preserve and use the shape of an event while the data is still in motion . You can explore individual event shapes, distinguish multiple event types within the same stream, and build processing logic against the event type you need. This works with events that reference registered schemas, events organized through classification, and untyped events whose structure is not yet defined. For developers working with mixed streams, this means building logic around each event type instead of repeatedly reconstructing its identity downstream. The event’s identity and shape become part of the streaming workflow, not just something to interpret after the data lands. Explore the events arriving in your stream When several event types share a feed, looking at the union of every field only tells part of the story. The schema-aware data preview feature organizes streaming data by event type, so you can focus on the shape you want to understand. For a thermostat event, you can inspect the fields describing temperature, humidity, location, and device state. Switch to an occupancy event, and the preview reflects fields for counts, zones, and observation time. To understand an unfamiliar event before configuring processing logic, inspect its payload, headers, and metadata, expand nested JSON, and open its individual details. Export selected data when you need to examine representative events further. More importantly, you can understand those differences while the stream is live , before building processing logic or waiting for the data to land somewhere else. Figure: Schema-aware data preview groups events with registered schemas (schematized events), classified events, and untyped events. Work with schemas at different levels of maturity Not every event producer is at the same point in its schema journey. Some applications publish against established, versioned contracts (schemas). Others already carry useful type information such as deviceType or eventType, but don’t have registered schemas. Still others produce events that are new, evolving, or not yet fully documented. Schema-aware Eventstreams lets those different events coexist in the same Eventstream through registered, classified, and untyped events. Schematized events: reuse established contracts For producers with defined contracts, schema-aware Eventstreams (Preview) can use schemas managed through Event SchemaSet, which is generally available, and Fabric’s Schema Registry. Events that reference these registered schemas are called schematized events. They use the CloudEvents format, with the ce_type header identifying the registered event type so Eventstreams can use the corresponding schema for exploration and processing. This gives producers and consumers an explicit, reusable definition of the event rather than deriving its meaning from whichever fields happen to appear in a sample. See how registered schemas work in Eventstreams . Classified events: find structure in existing streams Many useful streams don't start with registered contracts. A mixed JSON feed may already contain fields such as deviceType, eventType, or entityType that identify what each event represents. In the new Classifier workflow, select that field to organize the stream into distinct event types. In our building example, deviceType can separate thermostat, occupancy, air-quality, and badge-reader events even though they continue through the same Eventstream. Classification doesn't turn those events into registered contracts. It makes their existing structure usable for exploration and processing. Figure: The deviceType classifier separates a mixed stream into four event types with distinct detected fields. Untyped events: keep the unknown visible An event can still be inspected even when it has neither a registered schema nor a user-selected classifier. Untyped events keep that traffic visible without requiring you to define its structure first. Events from sources that aren’t associated with an Event SchemaSet can remain untyped or be organized through classification. In classified streams, events with a missing or null classifier value remain untyped. Events from schema-associated sources that fail validation are dropped and reported in runtime logs, not routed as untyped. This gives you room to inspect new or unmatched traffic and decide later whether it should be classified, registered, or continue as untyped. Build against each event, not the entire stream Seeing the different shapes is useful. Using those shapes while processing the stream is where schema awareness becomes especially powerful. Supported operators and destinations can select a registered, classified, or untyped event as their input. The fields available for configuration then correspond to that event shape rather than every field observed across the source. Suppose you want to identify high-temperature readings. That logic belongs to thermostat events. It shouldn't need to account for occupancy counts, badge identifiers, or air-quality attributes just because those events happen to travel through the same stream. For example, select the thermostat event as the input to the Filter operator and use its temperature field to identify high-temperature readings. That branch can focus on thermostat data, while occupancy, air-quality, and badge-reader events continue through the same Eventstream and follow their own processing paths. The same model extends to supported destinations such as Eventhouse, Lakehouse, custom endpoints, and derived streams. A destination can consume the selected event shape instead of treating a heterogeneous source as one undifferentiated feed. Figure: The Input schema list makes individual shapes available to the Filter operator. This shifts an important responsibility upstream. Instead of repeatedly reconstructing event type in downstream queries, applications, or transformations, the Eventstream itself can carry that processing context while the data is moving. Start where your data is today Adopting schemas doesn’t have to be the mandatory first step. Different producers have different owners, technologies, release schedules, and contract maturity. Requiring every producer to register a schema before you can distinguish event shapes can delay the value you expect from stream processing. Schema-aware Eventstreams lets you take a progressive approach: Register stable contracts that teams want to discover and reuse. Classify existing mixed feeds that already contain a meaningful type signal. Keep untyped traffic visible when its shape isn't known yet. Move toward registered contracts where stronger schema governance provides value. One Eventstream can therefore work with several event types and levels of schema maturity without forcing every producer to change at the same time. Start with the data you have today and introduce stronger contracts where they make sense. Schema-aware Eventstreams brings the meaning of an event into the streaming workflow itself. title: Create purpose-built custom visuals in Real-Time Dashboards with Copilot (Preview)
text: Real-Time Dashboards include built-in visuals for common monitoring and analysis scenarios. However, operational decisions do not always fit a standard chart. You may need to combine several signals, use a domain-specific layout, or present information differently for a particular workflow or audience. Custom visuals with Copilot, now in preview, help you create a dashboard experience around the operational question you need to answer. With custom visuals, you can describe the operational view you need in natural language. Copilot creates the supporting KQL query and HTML-based visualization directly in the dashboard, helping you move from an operational question to a tailored visual without first adapting the scenario to a predefined chart. Move beyond predefined chart types A standard chart starts with a visual type such as a line, bar, or pie chart. You then shape the query and formatting to fit that structure. This model works well when the question maps naturally to an established chart. Operational questions don't always fit that model. You might need a visual that combines several signals, uses a domain-specific layout, or presents status in a form that matches how your team works. Building that experience outside the dashboard can require front-end development and separate deployment and maintenance processes. Custom visuals begin with the outcome instead. Describe the operational question and the visual you want, and Copilot uses the selected database context to generate both the KQL query and an HTML-based visualization. The result is added directly to the dashboard as a new tile. Example: Turn venue metrics into an operational view Consider a venue operations dashboard that tracks wait times and ingress volume across several entrances. Standard KPI and chart visuals can show those measures individually, but an operator may need to understand how conditions differ across the venue. With a custom visual, the dashboard author can describe that operational view directly: arrange entrances spatially around the venue, show the current wait time and ingress volume for each entrance, and use color to highlight congestion. Copilot can then generate a visual design around that scenario. The result is not simply another way to plot the same data. It presents the information in a form designed around the operational question: Where is congestion building, and which entrance needs attention? Create a custom visual Start from a Real-Time Dashboard that you can edit, and that has its data sources to create a custom visual, open a Real-Time Dashboard that you can edit and confirm that its data sources are configured for custom visuals. In Editing mode, select Add visual > Describe a visual, enter your prompt, and submit it. Copilot adds the visual to the current dashboard page and generates the connected KQL query and HTML-based visualization Figure: In Editing mode, select Add visual, and then select Describe a visual to begin creating a custom visual. Figure: Copilot displays a generated KQL query and the connected custom visual in the dashboard. Review the first result as a starting point. The quality of the visual depends in part on how clearly the prompt communicates the question, the data to use, and the intended presentation. Figure: Review the generated entrance operations visual. Write a focused prompt A useful prompt gives Copilot enough context to choose the relevant data and design a visual that answers a specific question. Include the following details: The operational question: Explain the decision or condition that the visual should support. Measures: Name the values to calculate or compare, such as event count, latency, volume, or service state. Dimensions: Identify how to group or organize the results, such as location, service, category, or severity. Time range: Define the period that matters, such as the last hour or the last 24 hours. Presentation: Describe the visual form when you have a specific operational layout in mind. Interactions: Describe how viewers should explore the visual, such as displaying additional details or using controls to change what is shown. For example, you can ask Copilot to: Show the current operational status of each venue entrance. Display average wait time and ingress volume for each entrance and use color to make congestion immediately visible. Arrange the entrances spatially around the venue so operators can quickly identify where attention is needed. Create a storm monitoring view that positions storm events by latitude and longitude. Size each event based on severity and use color to distinguish warning levels. Show additional event details when a viewer explores an event. Create a service health board that shows each service and its dependencies as connected nodes. Use color to distinguish healthy, degraded, and critical services, and make critical services visually prominent so operators can quickly identify where investigation is needed. These prompts do more than name a chart. They describe the relationship between the data and the way a viewer should interpret it. You can make them more precise by adding the relevant measures, status rules, categories, or time window from your data. Review and refine the result Creating a custom visual is an iterative authoring experience. After Copilot creates the tile, review whether the visual answers the intended question and whether the generated query selects and aggregates the expected data. To make changes, select the Edit icon on the tile. In tile edit mode, you can review the query and the visual, then use the Copilot pane to refine either one. Follow-up prompts can clarify the original request without requiring you to start over. For example, you might narrow the time range, change the grouping, emphasize a service state, or adjust how the information is presented. Continue until the visual communicates the operational state clearly. Then select Apply , resize, or reposition the tile, and save the dashboard. Switch to viewing mode to confirm that the saved visual renders as expected in the experience your dashboard viewers use. This review step is important for AI-assisted authoring. Validate the generated query and visuals against your data and operational requirements. Clear labels, appropriate aggregation, and a focused visual hierarchy help viewers understand the result quickly. Next steps Start with an operational question that does not fit a standard chart. Describe the experience you need and use Copilot to create a first version that you can review and refine before sharing the dashboard. This approach helps you turn specialized monitoring needs into tailored operational views without building and maintaining a separate front-end experience. Learn how to configure the required identity and cloud connection, create a tile, write a focused prompt, and refine the result in Create a custom visual in a Real-Time Dashboard . Explore the built-in options in the Real-Time Dashboard visual gallery . Review formatting options for standard tiles in Customize Real-Time Dashboard visuals .

title: Incrementally migrate and re-migrate database objects with Migration Assistant for Fabric Warehouse (Preview)
text: Migrate database objects to Microsoft Fabric in phases without creating a new Warehouse for every run. Start with one business domain, add another when it is ready, or revisit an object after its source definition changes. You can also build on an existing Warehouse instead of replacing it. Incremental migration for Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview) lets you move workloads in manageable phases while keeping control of the destination. Select the objects required for the current workload, add more objects in later runs, and resolve naming conflicts when an incoming object already exists. The process migrates object definitions; it does not continuously synchronize changed rows. You can start with an empty Warehouse, continue a previous migration, or use an existing Warehouse that was not created through migration. This flexibility lets teams preserve completed work while adding the next approved scope. It also supports deliberate consolidation into the Fabric destinations that match your architecture. Choose the objects that belong in each migration Enterprise migration plans often span several teams, applications, and business domains. Those groups do not always need to move together. Incremental migration lets you define the scope of each run. Instead of including every source object, select the objects needed for the workload you are moving. For example, start with the schemas, tables, and views required by one business domain. Review the translated definitions and validate the dependent workload before expanding the scope. In a later run, return to the same Warehouse and add the next approved set of objects. In the destination Warehouse, open the Migration tab and select Get more objects . Provide the source connection or upload a supported source input, and then select Choose more objects to migrate to define the next set. Figure: Use Get more objects to start another migration run from the destination Warehouse. Figure: Select source objects and review dependencies and naming conflicts before migration. Before you start the run, review the complete object list populated in the selection dialog. The list flags naming conflicts and adds direct dependencies for selected objects. Confirm that every included object is necessary for the workload you intend to migrate. Filter source objects to show all objects, objects with naming conflicts, or objects without naming conflicts. Identify objects whose names already exist in the destination through warning indicators. Review each selected object’s direct dependencies before you start the migration. Migration Assistant includes those dependencies by default, so the final scope can contain more objects than you initially selected. Review the source, destination, selected objects, and included dependencies in the summary. Confirm that every object belongs in the current scope and that naming conflicts have an owner. The Migration Assistant guide for connecting to a source system describes the workflow. Build on an empty or existing warehouse The destination does not have to come from an earlier migration or a specific migration mode. Choose the destination based on the workload, ownership model, security boundary, and naming plan. The following starting points are supported. An empty Warehouse: Begin with a destination you have prepared and migrate the first set of objects into it. A previously migrated Warehouse: Add more objects or revisit selected objects from an earlier run. A Warehouse that was not created through migration: Bring source objects into a Warehouse that already contains work created through other means. You do not need to create another Warehouse just because you are starting another migration run. Reusing a destination can reduce unnecessary duplication and keep related objects together. Confirm, however, that the shared destination fits the workload and data-isolation requirements. Re-migrate objects with control Migration work often requires revisiting an earlier decision. A source definition can change after the first run, or a translated object might need correction after validation. Re-migration lets you return to that object without treating the entire source as a new migration. When an incoming object's name already exists in the destination, Migration Assistant identifies a naming conflict. Objects without naming conflicts can be created immediately. Conflicting objects remain pending and are not created or replaced until you explicitly choose how to resolve each conflict. For each conflict, compare the SQL definitions side by side: the existing definition on the left and the incoming translated definition on the right. Review the full definition, not only the highlighted difference, because connected changes can affect downstream objects. Then choose the action that fits the object. Keep existing: Retain the destination's current definition and discard the incoming translated definition. Keep incoming: Replace the existing definition with the incoming translated definition, confirming the action when prompted. Rename incoming: Create the incoming object under a different name while retaining the existing object. Conflict handling makes re-migration an explicit decision. You can preserve work already completed in Fabric, accept a revised source definition, or keep both definitions under different names. Record the chosen action so that workload owners understand which definition is active. Figure: Compare existing and incoming definitions before resolving a naming conflict. Replacing an object changes its definition in the destination and may require you to reload data or revalidate dependent workloads. Before you replace a table, view, or procedure, identify the objects and processes that use it and plan the required follow-up work. For detailed behavior, refer to Resolve conflicts and fix objects . Consolidate your data estate Incremental migration lets you move selected objects from supported SQL Server databases, Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pools, or Teradata databases into one or more Fabric Warehouses. A separate destination Warehouse is not required for every source database or migration run. The destination design should still reflect workload ownership, security, naming, and data-isolation requirements. This approach supports several consolidation patterns. Choose a pattern only after confirming that the workloads can share the same operational and security boundaries. Common uses are listed below. Consolidate objects from multiple databases on the same source platform. Bring together selected objects from different supported source platforms. Expand the same Warehouse as additional databases and workloads are ready to migrate. As you add objects, conflict handling helps you manage names already present in the destination. Compare existing and incoming definitions, then keep the existing object, replace it with the incoming definition, or rename the incoming object. This decision determines which definition becomes part of the consolidated Warehouse. Consolidating destinations does not automatically reconcile definitions or combine table data. Review dependencies, naming conventions, permissions, ownership, and data-loading requirements before each run. These checks help the consolidated Warehouse reflect the intended architecture rather than an accidental collection of objects. Keep object migration and data loading distinct In this preview, incremental migration means selecting, adding, or revisiting database object definitions across separate migration runs. It covers object selection, translation, dependency handling, and definition conflicts, but it does not continuously synchronize changed rows. After migrating the required definitions and resolving conflicts, plan the associated data movement.
